When optimized_pagination=true reaches this paginator, order_by="-datetime" makes value a datetime, so math.ceil(value)/math.floor(value) raises TypeError while building the first page cursor. Every authorized optimized audit-log request fails before returning rows. Use the same datetime-to-numeric conversion as DateTimePaginator instead of applying numeric rounding directly to the model field.

When an authorized request follows the first optimized page, OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the epoch-millisecond cursor integer directly, so BasePaginator.build_queryset compares the datetime column to that integer instead of converting it to a datetime; PostgreSQL then rejects the parameter or returns no matching rows, breaking cursor navigation. Convert the value with the same UTC datetime conversion used by DateTimePaginator.value_from_cursor.

Negative cursor offset is passed straight into queryset slicing. When a superuser or global-access member sends optimized_pagination=true with a cursor whose offset is negative (for example 0:-5:0), OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result uses cursor.offset unchanged in queryset[start_offset:stop]. Django querysets reject negative indexes with an AssertionError, which returns a 500.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is incompatible with datetime ordering used by the audit log endpoint. The endpoint orders by -datetime, but OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor or math.ceil directly on a datetime attribute. This raises TypeError when build_cursor builds the next and previous cursors. value_from_cursor also returns the raw integer cursor.value.

When an authorized caller submits a cursor with a negative offset, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result passes that offset directly to a Django QuerySet slice, so Django raises ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported and the audit-log request returns 500. Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets, and no endpoint validation prevents this trigger. Clamp the slice start to zero or reject negative offsets with BadPaginationError.

When a previous-page cursor contains a negative offset, BasePaginator.get_result preserves it and passes it to the Django QuerySet slice, which raises ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported and returns a 500. Cursor.from_string accepts negative offsets, so this is reachable through a client-supplied cursor even on the fallback DateTimePaginator path. Clamp the offset or reject it before slicing.

Prev-cursor trimming ignores the negative-offset start used for the slice. When cursor.is_prev is set, cursor.value is non-zero and the negative-offset branch ran, get_result compares len(results) with offset + limit + extra. That offset is the negative cursor.offset, and the slice was taken from start_offset. The comparison therefore never matches the real row count.

BasePaginator change still passes negative offsets for prev cursors, and its comment is misleading. In BasePaginator.get_result, start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset clamps only forward cursors. A user-supplied prev cursor with a negative offset, such as 0:-3:1, still reaches queryset[start_offset:stop] and raises an AssertionError, which returns a 500.

The only way to reach that class's negative-offset path is through a client-controlled cursor.

When a reschedule request returns or its worker is terminated before the async helper finishes, deleteScheduledEmailReminder/deleteScheduledSMSReminder can still be pending, so the old reminder remains uncancelled and the cron/provider can send it for the cancelled booking. Await both calls with Promise.all before completing the mutation.

When a workflow is deleted or edited, deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder calls are started without awaiting them, so the router can delete the workflow/step and return while provider cancellation or reminder-state persistence is still pending; a failure or race leaves the scheduled email/SMS deliverable.

When a cancelled SMS reminder falls within this window, scheduleEmailReminders sends its Twilio SID to SendGrid and then deletes the database row without calling Twilio, so the SMS is still delivered while its cancellation record is lost. Add method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL to this query, or move cancellation into a method-specific job.

When a scheduled reminder is cancelled after its scheduled time, the cancellation query cannot find it because the preceding deleteMany already removes every email reminder with scheduledDate <= now; the SendGrid cancellation is therefore never issued and the email can still be delivered. Process cancelled reminders before deleting expired rows, or exclude cancelled: true rows from that cleanup.

When SendGrid rejects one cancellation request, the for loop exits and the outer catch logs the error without processing any later reminders, so those cancelled bookings retain their scheduled emails and can still be sent until a later run succeeds. Handle each reminder's provider call and deletion independently so one failed cancellation cannot starve the rest.

When a booking has workflow reminders, the loop starts the asynchronous cancellation calls without awaiting them, so the handler can return success while cancelled is still false and the SendGrid/Twilio operation is still pending; the next reminder cron can then send the email.

When rescheduling a booking with existing reminders, the async cancellation calls are not awaited, so eventManager.reschedule and the new booking flow proceed while the old reminder is still active; a reminder worker can send the old notification after the reschedule.

When SendGrid rejects the immediate cancellation during rescheduling, deleteScheduledEmailReminder catches the error internally and leaves this reminder neither cancelled nor retryable, so the old workflow email remains scheduled and can be sent for the replaced booking. Remove the true argument so the reminder is marked cancelled and the cron job can retry the provider cancellation.

Reminder cancellation is a floating promise, so the DB write may never run. When a booking is cancelled, deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await or collection into the Promise.all below.

Reschedule uses immediateDelete, which still hits the SendGrid 100-cancellation limit and is never retried. When a booking is rescheduled, deleteScheduledEmailReminder calls the SendGrid cancel endpoint directly, and if the call fails, the error is swallowed inside the manager and the row is not marked for retry.

One failing SendGrid cancel aborts all remaining cancellations and blocks the queue. In the remindersToCancel loop, client.request is awaited inside a single try around the whole loop, so if one cancel throws, the loop exits and remaining cancelled reminders are skipped.

When a reschedule contains calendar or video references, the async callback returns a promise that forEach ignores, so the mutation sends the reschedule email and webhook before deletion completes and any deletion rejection becomes an unhandled floating promise. This leaves the old provider event/meeting active while the booking has moved on. Replace this with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) (or await a sequential loop) before sending notifications.

When any optional integration chunk fails to load, the appStore initialization creates a rejected promise for that entry without attaching a rejection handler, so Node can report an unhandled rejection or terminate the process even if no request uses that integration. Wrap imports in deferred, handled loaders or attach centralized rejection handling before exposing the registry.

When a booking has a calendar or video reference, Reschedule starts the asynchronous deletion inside forEach without awaiting its callback, so deletion rejections bypass the surrounding try/catch, the reschedule email is sent before deletion completes, and the function returns success while the provider event can remain. Replace this with await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...)) (or a sequential for...of) and await each delete call.

When a booking has calendar or video references, Reschedule starts each async deletion inside forEach but does not await the callbacks, so it sends the reschedule email and returns before external cleanup completes; rejected deletions also bypass this try/catch as unhandled rejections. Await Promise.all (or a sequential loop) over the deletion promises before sending the email.

When a recurring booking cancellation enters this branch, the async forEach callback does not finish before Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) runs, so calendar.deleteEvent promises can be omitted and external events remain after cancellation. Replace the forEach with an awaited for...of loop or collect and await the callback promises.

forEach(async) leaves deletes as floating promises that the try/catch cannot catch in Reschedule, the callback passed to bookingRefsFiltered.forEach is now async and awaits getCalendar. forEach ignores the returned promises, so calendar?.deleteEvent and deleteMeeting run unawaited. Async forEach pushes into apiDeletes after Promise.all has already been awaited. When two mark_failed calls for the same environment overlap while monitor_env.status is still OK, try_incident_threshold lets both workers pass the check, save ERROR, retrieve the same active incident, and publish occurrences for the same check-ins, while also emitting monitor_environment_failed twice. Add a row lock or conditional status update and only run these side effects for the worker that won the transition.

When create_incident_occurrence raises after the environment is saved as ERROR, try_incident_threshold exits without recording or retrying the occurrence for that triggering check-in; there is no sweep selecting errored environments, and later processing only handles newly received failures. A failed final check-in can therefore leave the incident without its occurrence. Enclose the transition and durable work in a retryable transaction or persist an outbox/retry record before marking the environment errored.

When a monitor has fewer than failure_issue_threshold recorded check-ins and all of them are failures, try_incident_threshold treats the short list as having reached the threshold, so a first failure can create an incident even when the configured threshold is 8. This violates the configured consecutive-count contract and publishes an issue prematurely. Require len(previous_checkins) >= failure_issue_threshold before changing the environment to ERROR.

Schedule-type display conversion is computed but never used - when a monitor config has schedule_type, get_monitor_environment_context copies it into the local config and swaps in the display string, but the returned dict uses monitor_environment.monitor.config, so the converted copy is dead and the occurrence's monitor context shows the raw numeric schedule_type instead of the readable value.
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for SpawnProcess, so hung flushers are never killed because SpawnProcess subclasses BaseProcess, not multiprocessing.context.Process
When --flusher-processes=-1 is supplied, SpanFlusher computes num_processes=-1, creates no process-map entries, and raises KeyError while assigning the first shard, preventing consumer startup
A value of 0 for --flusher-processes is silently treated as unlimited by max_processes or len(...), violating the option's maximum-processes contract
When SpanFlusher is constructed without max_processes, self.max_processes becomes the number of assigned shards, starting one worker per shard instead of the documented default of one

When produce_to_pipe is configured and a worker thread is deemed unhealthy, _ensure_processes_alive starts a replacement without stopping or joining the old thread, potentially causing duplicate segment payloads
join() skips terminating remaining processes once the deadline passes because the break at remaining_time <= 0 check prevents later processes from being waited on or terminated
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched with lambda _: None, making the test depend on thread scheduling and potentially flaky

When result_processor raises in OrderedQueueWorker.run, the finally block marks the Kafka offset complete, so _commit_loop commits a message whose side effect failed and the result is not retried. Preserve failed offsets as outstanding and retry them or route them through an explicit failure/dead-letter path before committing.

When decoder or grouping_fn raises in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, this handler marks the message complete after only logging the exception, so _commit_loop can acknowledge an unprocessed result and discard it. Leave failed offsets uncommitted or send them through an explicit retry/dead-letter path; only complete offsets for intentionally skipped messages.

When Arroyo closes this strategy during partition reassignment, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close shuts down the factory-shared self.queue_pool but leaves ResultsStrategyFactory.queue_pool non-None; the next strategy then submits to shut-down queues, catches queue.ShutDown, and marks messages complete without processing them. Recreate the pool for each strategy or move pool shutdown exclusively to ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown.

Strategy close/terminate shuts down the factory-shared queue pool, so messages are dropped after a rebalance. When Arroyo revokes partitions during a rebalance, it calls close/join/terminate on the strategy, so SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls queue_pool.shutdown(). The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused by every create_thread_queue_parallel_worker call.

When ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown runs with queued work, FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets each worker's shutdown flag before closing the queues, so workers finish only their current item and leave queued messages unprocessed; the commit thread is also stopped first. The consumer therefore exits without processing or committing those messages, causing graceful shutdown to drop in-flight work and replay it later.

When FixedQueuePool.shutdown runs with queued work, setting each worker's shutdown flag makes OrderedQueueWorker.run stop before consuming remaining items, despite the subsequent queue.shutdown(immediate=False) requesting a graceful drain. Consumer shutdown therefore drops queued results and stops the workers before their side effects run.

When result processing is slower than submission, FixedQueuePool uses an unbounded queue.Queue, so every fetched message and decoded result can accumulate in memory while submit never blocks. Sustained backlog can exhaust the consumer process instead of applying the advertised backpressure. Construct bounded queues and make a full queue pause or otherwise backpressure Kafka polling.

When a Kafka partition contains a gap in offsets, OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets stops at the first absent integer and never advances past it, even after later messages complete. Kafka offsets can be non-contiguous, so this leaves commits permanently stalled and causes completed results to be replayed after restart.

When uptime result processing is slower than Kafka delivery, ResultsStrategyFactory creates FixedQueuePool with unbounded queue.Queue instances, so SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit keeps accepting messages without backpressure and retains the backlog in process memory until the worker catches up. This can cause unbounded memory growth during a sustained slowdown.

When Arroyo invokes join with a finite timeout, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join ignores it and calls close, which can block for the fixed five-second commit-thread join plus five-second worker joins regardless of the caller's deadline. This can exceed the consumer's configured rebalance/shutdown join timeout and delay partition handoff.

When SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy delivers the five same-group messages out of order, test_preserves_order_within_group still passes because it asserts only the count, so the queue's ordering guarantee can regress without detection. Assert the recorded subscription sequence.

When FixedQueuePool is replaced by a serial worker or all groups are processed through one blocking path, test_concurrent_processing_different_groups still passes because it waits for completion and checks only the final count, so the claimed parallelism is untested. Add a barrier-based processor that blocks one group while asserting another group can enter.

When a worker drains all ten submissions before get_stats() runs, test_stats_reporting fails even though FixedQueuePool is functioning correctly, because submit is asynchronous and get_stats() reports current queued items only. Synchronize on a processor barrier or otherwise hold a submitted item in the worker before asserting the queue statistics.

When FixedQueuePool assigns both subscriptions to one worker or the implementation processes them serially, test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions still passes because it only waits for two calls and checks their count. Add a barrier/in-flight counter in the mocked processor and assert both calls overlap.

When the first worker raises and the second message succeeds, test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that no offset was committed, contradicting its claim that errors do not block commits for other messages. OrderedQueueWorker.run calls complete_offset in finally even after an exception, so the current implementation can commit offset 101 and fail this test.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, and revoked partitions are not handled. _commit_loop runs on its own thread and calls commit_function, which wraps the Arroyo StreamProcessor commit callback. Arroyo's consumer and commit state are meant to be driven from the processing thread, so this races with poll/submit. OffsetTracker also keeps no per-partition cleanup.

Commit scan stops at any non-contiguous offset, so one gap blocks commits for that partition. When offsets in a partition are not contiguous (transaction markers, compaction, or FilteredPayload messages that never reach submit), get_committable_offsets breaks at the first offset missing from all_offsets.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure never happens. The class docstring promises natural backpressure when queues fill up. FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit never raises MessageRejected.

Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and passes only because of timing. The docstring of test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says errors don't block offset commits. The test then asserts that no commit for test_partition has happened.
